title: Elliot and the Rogue Geyser
markdown:
Elliot Nocturne. That name sounds like midnight shadows and secrets, doesn't it? But Elliot wasn't quite living up to it. He was a vampire, a real cape-wearing, coffin-sleeping one. And guess what? He was on probation. He lived in a house that was just too white, with a mailbox sporting a tiny plastic flamingo. An affront to all things nocturnal and dignified. His biggest problems used to be dodging sunlight and finding a good vintage of O-negative. Now? Now it was avoiding Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning petunias and remembering to put his recycling out on the correct Tuesday. Not just any Tuesday, oh no. The second Tuesday of the month, unless it was a leap year, then it was the third, but only if the moon was waxing gibbous. Honestly, the sheer effort of it all was enough to make a creature of the night want to turn into a bat and fly away forever.

“This is a nightmare,” he’d mutter, smoothing his perpetually rumpled tweed vest. The fabric strained against his shadowy frame. “A pastel-colored, lawn-mowing nightmare. With passive-aggressive garden gnomes.”

And then there was Mina Brightwood. Mina! She was the daylight consultant assigned to Elliot. Consultant. It sounded so important, didn't it? Like she had a degree in something immeasurably important. But really, Mina was like a human ray of sunshine with glitter sprinkled on top. Her hair was the color of a canary’s sneeze – a truly blinding shade of yellow. Her smile was so wide it could swallow your whole head and then offer you a cookie. She was impossibly organized; her handbag probably contained a color-coded filing system for her lip gloss.

“Good morning, Elliot!” she’d chirp, her voice like tiny bells tinkling in a hurricane. This was usually at three in the afternoon, when Elliot was desperately trying to find a dark sock that didn't smell faintly of dust mites. “Ready to tackle the day with gusto?”

Elliot would usually grunt, pulling his scarf tighter. “Gusto is for mortals, Mina. I prefer… dignified lethargy. And perhaps a nice cup of… well, you know.” He’d gesture vaguely towards his perpetually half-empty blood bag stash.

“Dignified lethargy isn’t on the probation checklist, dear!” she’d giggle, tapping a ridiculously long list with a bright pink pen that looked suspiciously like a magic wand. “We’ve got ‘Civic Engagement’ and ‘Positive Community Contribution’ coming up! And remember, no more nocturnal lawn mowing! The neighbors complained it sounded like a swarm of angry bees being attacked by a lawnmower!”

And that’s how Elliot found himself, on a Tuesday evening that felt like a thousand years long, crammed into a folding chair at the community hall. The air smelled faintly of stale biscuits, mothballs, and the lingering scent of desperation from too many people trying to live up to suburban perfection. This was the infamous Neighborhood Watch meeting. Elliot felt like a black hole at a glitter convention.

“Alright, alright, settle down, everyone!” boomed Mr. Henderson, the self-appointed head of the Neighborhood Watch. He wore a bright orange vest that screamed, “I have too much time on my hands! And also, I secretly wear a cape!” Elliot was convinced Mr. Henderson was just practicing for his eventual superhero career, which would probably involve enforcing curfews and making sure everyone watered their lawns to the correct height.

Elliot slumped lower in his plastic chair, trying to become one with the beige walls. He could practically hear his ancestors groaning in their dusty crypts, their ghostly moans whispering, “Elliot, what are you doing to our noble lineage?”

“Now,” Mr. Henderson continued, pointing a stern, slightly trembling finger at a slightly lopsided garden gnome in the corner. This gnome, Reginald, had seen better days. His painted-on smile was chipped, and one of his tiny ceramic boots was missing. “We have had… incidents.” He drew the word out like it was a particularly nasty spider. “Mrs. Gable’s prize-winning gnome, Reginald, was… repositioned last night. Facing the fence. A clear act of gnome-related aggression!”

A chorus of gasps rippled through the room, a wave of indignant murmurs. Elliot blinked. Reginald? Facing the fence? Was this serious? He’d always thought Reginald looked a bit shifty anyway, with that knowing glint in his ceramic eyes.

“And don’t even get me started on the recycling bins!” squeaked Mrs. Higgins, her face turning a shade of puce that rivaled Elliot’s least favorite shade of burgundy. She clutched her pearls. “Someone – and I’m not naming names, but I’m looking at you, Mr. Fitzwilliam, with your suspiciously empty bin! – put their banana peels in the glass bin again!” She shuddered dramatically.

Elliot suppressed a shudder of his own. Banana peels. The indignity. He’d always found fruit rather… messy. The thought of it mingling with perfectly good glass bottles made his fangs ache. He made a mental note to never, ever have a banana in his vicinity.

Suddenly, a WHOOSH and a SPLASH echoed from outside, followed by a sound that could only be described as a frustrated gurgle. Everyone jumped. Mr. Henderson’s eyes narrowed to laser-like slits. “What in the Sam Hill was that?” he boomed, his voice vibrating with suspicion.

Elliot’s heart sank like a lead balloon filled with cobwebs. He’d been trying to water his tiny, pathetic patch of graveyard dirt in the backyard – a concession to his probation, which stated he must engage in “responsible horticultural practices.” But his ancient, leaky vampire watering can, inherited from a particularly eccentric great-aunt, had a mind of its own. It had apparently decided to aim for the heavens, or perhaps a passing cloud. Now, a rogue geyser was erupting from his hose, spraying water in a magnificent arc that was heading directly for Mrs. Gable's meticulously pruned rose bushes. And, judging by the trajectory, it was going to drench Mr. Henderson’s prize-winning (and suspiciously brown) lawn too. Oh, and Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning gnome, Reginald, who was currently sitting on the edge of his own little gnome-patio.

“Oh, fiddlesticks,” Elliot mumbled, trying to melt into the beige walls, which was a challenge given his inherent dramatic flair and tendency to wear slightly too-dark clothing.

Mina, bless her sunshiny heart, was already on her feet. She didn’t walk; she practically bounced. “Goodness gracious! That looks like a plumbing predicament!” she declared, her voice cutting through the hushed panic like a perfectly aimed laser beam. “Don’t you worry, everyone! I’ll just nip out and sort this out! Probably a loose washer!” She was already halfway to the door.

Before Elliot could even protest – and he really wanted to, because "sorting things out" in his vampire way usually involved a lot more chaos – Mina was out the door, a blur of yellow and relentless optimism. Elliot watched through the grimy window, a strange mix of dread and a tiny, almost imperceptible flicker of… something else. He’d made a mess. A big, splashy, gnome-and-recycling-bin-adjacent mess. He was doomed. More probation violations meant more compulsory attendance at the local craft fair, and the thought of that was truly terrifying.

Then, something amazing happened. Mina, with a series of rapid, cheerful instructions that sounded like she was conducting a symphony of garden tools, and what looked like a strategically placed, slightly dented watering can lid, managed to wrangle the rogue geyser into submission. She didn’t just stop it; she redirected it. With a flick of her wrist and a surprisingly strong kick, she managed to aim the spray so it was now enthusiastically watering Mr. Henderson’s suspiciously brown lawn and, as a bonus, giving Reginald the gnome a much-needed bath. The whole thing took about thirty seconds. Thirty seconds! Elliot, who had spent centuries mastering the art of shapeshifting into a bat, couldn’t even manage to water his own dirt without causing an international incident. He was officially humbled by a woman with sunshine hair.

He shuffled out of the hall, dragging his feet like he was walking through a bog of forgotten socks. Mina met him by the entrance, her face glowing like a freshly polished silver spoon, not a drop of water on her.

“All sorted, Elliot!” she said, beaming, her smile practically blinding him. “Just a little… garden excitement! You know, sometimes things just get a bit… enthusiastic, don’t they? Like a boisterous puppy that needs a little gentle guidance!”

Elliot just stared at her, his pale face a mask of bewildered defeat. “Enthusiastic?” he croaked, the word feeling foreign and ridiculous on his tongue. “It was a catastrophic flood! Mrs. Gable will be inconsolable about Reginald’s damp hat!”

Mina linked her arm through his, somehow managing to avoid his perpetually cold skin with practiced ease. “Exactly! And isn’t it wonderful how we can all come together to help? That’s what community is all about! Helping each other out when the sprinklers go rogue or the banana peels go astray!” She nudged him gently. “You were trying, Elliot. That’s what counts! And next time, perhaps we can work on a more… controlled watering system. Something less… geyser-like.”

Elliot looked at the little white house, the flamingo mailbox which was now shimmering under the streetlights, and the still-slightly-damp pavement that smelled vaguely of petunias and regret. He looked at Mina, her face glowing like a beacon of pure, unadulterated cheerfulness. He still hated gardening. He still thought recycling was a complex human conspiracy designed to drive him insane. And he still yearned for the quiet darkness of his coffin, where the only noise was the gentle creak of ancient wood. But as he mumbled a grudging, "Thank you, Mina," he realized that maybe, just maybe, this suburban nightmare wasn’t quite as unbearable as he thought. Especially when you had a consultant who could wrangle rogue geysers with the power of pure, unadulterated cheerfulness and a well-placed watering can lid. Now that was a superpower. A genuinely useful superpower. Perhaps, just perhaps, probation wouldn't be so bad after all. As long as Mina was around to manage the neighborhood's rampant enthusiasm.
characters: Elliot the suburban vampire on probation, Mina the daylight consultant
